segments.title: The Fog and What It Hides: Opening Bleak House

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, unhurried reading of one of the greatest novels in the English language.

I'm your host, and over the course of this series we're going to move through Bleak House chapter by chapter — its fogs, its lawsuits, its orphans, its monsters, and its moments of devastating beauty.
Three remarkable readers are joining me today, and I want to introduce each of them properly.

Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels for audio than almost anyone alive — he comes to Dickens as a performer, listening for the comic timing, the grotesque energy, the moments written to be heard rather than read.

Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of power — every institution in Bleak House, the law, philanthropy, the aristocracy, is a mechanism, and Daniel will show us exactly what it produces.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since she was a teenager — she brings the deep intimacy of a reader who keeps returning, and strong opinions about who deserves better.
So — Bleak House.
A novel of fog and interminable legal proceedings, yes — but also one of the most richly populated, formally audacious, and emotionally violent works ever written.
Oliver, you've read this novel aloud more times than most people have read it silently — where does it begin for you?
It begins, I always think, as a kind of provocation.
Dickens opens the throttle on atmosphere so completely that you forget, for a page or two, that there are any human beings in the book at all.
And then he drops you into a room — and the room tells you everything.
Take Skimpole's sitting room, which we encounter later in the novel.
Esther describes it like this:
And then — hothouse nectarines on the table, grapes, sponge-cakes, and a bottle of light wine.
While a broken pane of glass is merely papered over.
That is Skimpole in a single room — all appetite, no repair.
What I love about that passage is the precision of the accumulation.
Dickens doesn't just say the room is contradictory — he lists.
Footstool, sofa, cushions, easy-chair, pillows, piano, books, drawing materials — and you're counting the comforts even as you register the squalor.
And then Skimpole himself, reclining in his dressing-gown, drinking fragrant coffee from old china, looking at wallflowers.
It's mid-day. He is entirely at his ease. The world may do as it likes.
And yet later, at the darkest hours of the novel, the atmosphere shifts completely — there's a passage assigned to Oliver involving George Rouncewell keeping watch that I find almost unbearable.
Yes — and the contrast is everything, isn't it.
George Rouncewell, the old soldier, sitting through the long remainder of a blank wintry night beside Sir Leicester.
And then dawn comes, and listen to how Dickens renders it.
That phrase — 'who will tell him' — is almost operatic in its repetition.
The day itself is the messenger of catastrophe, and it arrives colourless, as if ashamed.
There's something worth holding onto there — the way the darkness in that scene is the shadow of an institution, not just a weather event.
Chancery casts its darkness across every threshold in this novel.
Esther Summerson says something, when reflecting on Gridley, that strikes me as the novel's most honest statement of what the law actually does to people.
She's speaking through Richard's farewell words, and the voice she hears is Gridley's:
Chancery has not broken — that's the formulation.
Everything else — family, hope, human connection — has been severed by the court.
The only bond left is a bond of shared suffering — and that, Chancery cannot touch, because it has already destroyed everything else.
That list — 'of all my old associations, of all my old pursuits and hopes, of all the living and the dead world' — it's like watching someone empty their pockets.
Everything that constitutes a life — and then at the end of the inventory, one person remains.
And the reason that one person remains is not love or good fortune — it's that Chancery has not yet found a way to break that particular tie.
It's an indictment dressed as consolation. That's a devastating thing to write.
And what's remarkable is that this devastation arrives in a novel that is also frequently, genuinely hilarious.
Skimpole reclining on his sofa with his nectarines, and a broken window papered over — that is comedy of a very high order.
Dickens holds both registers in the same hand simultaneously — and never drops either one.
That dual register — the comic and the catastrophic — is going to be one of the threads running through this entire series.
And what I think we've already established, just in these opening passages, is that Bleak House is a novel in which atmosphere is never decorative — it is always diagnostic.
The fog, the phantom dawn, the room full of cushions and broken glass — they are telling us, from the first page, exactly what kind of world this is.
Coming up — we'll go deeper into the characters themselves, and ask what Bleak House really thinks about who suffers and who escapes.

segments.title: The Law as Machine: Class, Property, and the Chancery

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel apart chapter by chapter — and puts it back together again.
I'm your host, and today we're looking at what may be the novel's most enduring obsession: the law — specifically the Court of Chancery — as a machine for class power.
To dig into that, I'm joined by three guests who each bring a quite distinct angle to this material.

Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels on audio than arguably any living person, and he hears Dickens the way a composer hears a score — in the rhythms, the timing, the performance built into the prose itself.
Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every institution in a Dickens novel as a mechanism of class power — and he is, I can tell you, not gentle about Chancery.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and devoted re-reader of Bleak House, who cares above all about the experience on the page — what moves you, what makes you laugh, what makes you stop and read a line again.
Let's begin with Lawrence Boythorn, who I think is one of Dickens's great comic gifts to us — a man at perpetual war with his neighbour Sir Leicester Dedlock over a right of way.
Daniel, you've written about how the law in this novel serves property and rank above everything else — and I think Boythorn is a fascinating case study in that.
Boythorn is one of those passages where Dickens is being funnier than he perhaps intends — and more radical than he knows.
On the surface it's pure comic performance — this magnificent blusterer firing volleys at the aristocracy.
But look at what the dispute actually is: it's a right of way.
It's about who has the legal claim to walk across a piece of ground — and Sir Leicester's answer is that it's his ground because it belongs to the park of Chesney Wold.
What Dickens shows us — through the comedy — is that the law doesn't adjudicate between equals.
It recycles the privilege of those who already own the landscape.
And what makes Boythorn delightful is that he refuses to accept that — he just meets legal action with legal action, and physical force with physical force.
Listen to the rhythm when Dickens finally lets him reach his triumphant conclusion — it's worth reading aloud.
"He brings actions for trespass; I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha, ha!"
That triple rhythm — he does this, I do that — it's the structure of a legal duel rendered as pure farce.
And what Boythorn understands — instinctively — is that if Sir Leicester can use the law, so can he.
The system only begins to feel neutral when both parties have equal resources to fight it.
Daniel, you've made it sound almost theoretical — but the sheer pleasure of that passage is in the escalation.
A fire engine, man traps, split peas fired at legs — Dickens is building a comic set piece that would work on a stage.
And the formal letters between them — that is the genius of it.
"Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, presents his compliments" — and then Boythorn fires back with exactly the same stiff formality.

"Mr. Lawrence Boythorn presents his compliments to Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, and has to call HIS attention to the fact that he totally denies the whole of Sir Leicester Dedlock's positions on every possible subject."
That capitalised HIS — which is Dickens on the page, but when you perform it, you simply lean on that pronoun and the audience erupts.
It's a masterclass in using the language of deference as a weapon.
And what I love about Boythorn as a creation — he's not a victim of the system at all.
He's a man who can afford to fight, and he fights with magnificent, total commitment.
What strikes me is that Dickens frames the whole confrontation through Boythorn's reported speech — we never hear Sir Leicester's side directly.
Which means we get Boythorn's theatrical version of events, full of abandoned villains with one eye and execrable scoundrels.
But I think that choice is pointed — Sir Leicester speaks through lawyers and agents and letters.
He doesn't have to be present because the system speaks for him.
Boythorn, by contrast, is physically everywhere — with his fire engine, his axe, his man traps.
One character occupies the landscape in person; the other occupies it through property law.
And Dickens — through the comedy — is showing us that those are not equivalent forms of power.
That distinction — the body versus the deed of ownership — is a quietly devastating one.
Now, if Boythorn is the comic version of fighting the system, Jarndyce represents something altogether more weary — a man who has simply withdrawn from Chancery on moral grounds.
Daniel, you've been assigned a passage late in the novel where Jarndyce finally articulates why he refuses to engage with the suit.
Yes, and it's a passage I find both admirable and — I have to say — a little too comfortable.
Jarndyce has made a private moral decision: he will have nothing to do with Chancery.
And the novel endorses him — he's one of the few genuinely good men in the book.
But what does personal withdrawal actually achieve?
When a will is discovered late in the proceedings, he won't even read it — he won't touch it.
And his explanation is this — I want to read it carefully, because it's one of the most loaded sentences in the novel.
"The plain truth is, I have forsworn and abjured the whole business these many years, and my soul is sick of it."
"My soul is sick of it" — that is a man describing a spiritual wound, not a political position.
And the novel, to its credit, never lets us forget that Jarndyce's withdrawal doesn't save Richard Carstone.
The suit devours Richard regardless of whether the good man keeps his hands clean.
That phrase — "forsworn and abjured" — is extraordinary to read aloud.
Those are legal words — the language of the court itself — turned against the court.
Jarndyce is using the vocabulary of oaths and renunciations to make his personal break feel absolute.
And then "my soul is sick of it" drops the register entirely — suddenly we're in the plain vernacular.
It's a miniature of how Dickens works — the elevated and the blunt side by side, and the blunt one always lands harder.
Daniel is right that Jarndyce's withdrawal doesn't protect Richard — but I think Dickens is quite deliberate about that.
Richard's tragedy is precisely that he can't perform that act of renunciation.
He can't say — my soul is sick of this — and mean it and move on.
The suit becomes his vocation — a terrible dark mirror of the genuine vocation that the novel prizes.
Mrs. Badger says it plainly in an earlier scene, comparing Richard to young Woodcourt.
She notes that Richard lacks — and I'm reading now — "that positive interest in it which makes it his vocation."
Without vocation, every path becomes equally available — and equally unreal.
And into that vacancy, the suit rushes.
That's true — but I'd push it one step further.
The novel is rather cruel about Richard — it frames his failure as essentially a failure of character and will.
But Chancery is a system designed to create exactly this kind of paralysis.
The suit has dangled before Richard's family for generations — it's not weakness that makes him susceptible, it's context.
Dickens gives us all the structural conditions for Richard's destruction and then blames his soul.
That tension — between systemic cause and individual character — is one Dickens never quite resolves, is it.
There's a passage later in the novel I'd like to bring in now — one that shows us class working not through courts but through emotional blackmail of a very particular kind.
Daniel, you've been assigned Mrs. Rouncewell's extraordinary speech to Lady Dedlock — in which a loyal servant has to beg an aristocrat to act with common human decency.
This is one of the passages in the novel that I find hardest to read — not because it's badly written, quite the contrary.
Mrs. Rouncewell's son George has been falsely accused of murder, and she comes to Lady Dedlock because she believes, correctly, that her mistress knows something relevant.
Now — what should this scene look like in a just world?
A woman knows evidence that could exonerate an innocent man — she produces it.
But Mrs. Rouncewell cannot compel Lady Dedlock.
She has no legal standing, no social leverage — so she has to beg.
And look at how precisely she has to calibrate that plea — first flattering her mistress, then gently accusing her, then pleading again.

"My Lady, you may have some proud or angry reasons for disdaining to utter something that you know; if so, pray, oh, pray, think of a faithful servant whose whole life has been passed in this family which she dearly loves."
She has to acknowledge that Lady Dedlock might have reasons — she has to grant the lady's right to have proud or angry reasons — before she can even ask her to set them aside.
That is the texture of class deference — and it is indistinguishable from a form of coercion directed at the person with less power.
What moves me about that speech — and it does move me, every time — is Mrs. Rouncewell's total clarity about the social architecture she's operating inside.
She says: you are "by nature so high and distant" that you may not understand what a mother feels.
That is — at one level — a compliment delivered with exquisite care.
At another level it is a quiet accusation: your elevation has made you less than fully human.
Dickens calls her plea one of "genuine simplicity" — but it is also enormous sophistication.
She knows exactly what she's doing.
The rhythm of that speech is extraordinary to perform — it spirals inward, clause after clause, the way genuine desperation actually sounds.
"Pray, oh, pray" — that repetition — it's not rhetorical flourish, it's the grammatical form of a person running out of options.
And Dickens frames it — the omniscient narrator frames it — with that note about "genuine simplicity," as if to insist: don't read this as manipulation.
But the tragedy is that it has to be both.
She has to deploy every rhetorical resource she possesses in order to exercise what should be the most basic human claim — protect an innocent man.
That image — deploying rhetoric in order to exercise a basic human right — feels very central to what this novel is doing.
Before we close, I want to bring in one more passage — a smaller one, but I think a telling counterweight.
There's a late scene where Ada kneels beside the dying Richard — and Caroline, I'd love to know what you make of that moment against everything we've been discussing.
It's the quietest possible rebuke to everything the law has done.
Chancery has taken years from Richard, hollowed him out, and brought him here — and Ada simply kneels down.
The passage is almost unbearably visual — Dickens gives it to us in one long flowing clause, as if the image has to arrive whole.
"my darling rose, put off her bonnet, kneeled down beside him with her golden hair falling like sunlight on his head, clasped her two arms round his neck, and turned her face to me."
The sunlight — that word — in a novel so full of fog and mud and the darkness of Chancery.
It's the novel insisting that devotion and love are still real — even when the system has taken everything else.
That image will stay with you.
The golden hair falling like sunlight — it has the quality of a painting, or a tableau, the kind of thing that in Dickens's day might have been staged as a living picture.
And Esther is there — turning to face Esther — so the tenderness is witnessed and held.
When a novel has earned that moment, it's almost impossible not to feel it — however many times you've read it.
I don't want to be the person who refuses to feel that — because I feel it too.
But I think we have to hold it alongside the fact that the Chancery suit is shortly to be revealed as having consumed itself in costs — leaving nothing for anyone.
The beauty of that image is real — and it exists in a world where the machine runs on regardless.
The machine runs on regardless — that's perhaps as good a summary of the novel's view of Chancery as any single phrase could offer.
My thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, Daniel Rosen, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that has done exactly what this novel demands — it has made us think and feel at the same time.
In our next segment, we'll be moving deeper into the novel's treatment of identity and secrecy — the hidden histories that the Chancery system both produces and conceals.

segments.title: Comic Grotesques and the Art of Voice

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the show where we take one of the great English novels apart — carefully, lovingly, and with full attention to why it still matters.
I'm joined today by three remarkable readers who each bring something distinct to the table.
Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more classic audiobooks than any living performer — he hears Dickens the way a musician hears a score, and he'll be our guide to the novel's extraordinary verbal music.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian whose eye goes straight to what institutions do to people — he reads every comic scene as a symptom of something urgent.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with Bleak House since her teens — she brings the reader's intimate, hard-won devotion to every page.
Today we're focusing on Dickens's comic grotesques — the vivid, strange, occasionally monstrous creations that make this novel unlike anything else in English fiction.
Oliver, you've spent more time inside Dickens's prose than almost anyone alive — where do we even begin?
We begin, I think, exactly where Dickens begins — which is in the fog.
Because what Dickens does in those opening pages is something no other novelist had quite attempted — he builds an atmosphere so thick and particular it becomes a character in its own right.
When I first read it aloud — really performed it — I remember stopping and thinking: this is incantation, not description.
The passage begins — and I do want to read this because it's simply glorious —

"Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city."
That parenthetical — "and dirty" — is the joke buried inside the sublime.
He's been building this magnificent Gothic atmosphere and then he simply winks at you.
That's Dickens's genius — the grotesque and the comic are never more than a syllable apart.
What strikes me every time is that it's also a list of the suffering — and the list keeps descending the social scale.
You start with grand geography — rivers, marshes, great ships — and you end with a shivering apprentice boy on deck.
"Fog cruelly pinching the toes and fingers of his shivering little 'prentice boy on deck."
The word "cruelly" — it lands so quietly, and yet it changes everything.
The fog isn't just atmosphere at that point — it's actively doing harm to the smallest, most powerless person in the scene.
Dickens hides enormous feeling inside what looks like rhetorical display.
Caroline is right — and I'd push that a step further.
The fog is doing what Chancery does throughout the novel — it penetrates everywhere, it afflicts everyone, but it does not afflict everyone equally.
The ancient Greenwich pensioners wheeze by their firesides — they at least have firesides.
The boy on deck has nothing between him and the weather but his own skin.
So yes, it's magnificent prose — but the structure of the prose is also the structure of class society.
That's a remarkable convergence — aesthetic, moral, and political all at once, and in the first paragraph of the novel.
Oliver, let's move into the comic portraits — because Bleak House is also one of the funniest novels in the language, and some of those laughs come from very dark places indeed.
The Pardiggle boys.
I mean — if you want Dickens at the height of his grotesque comedy, look no further.
Esther observes them with this wonderfully precise, almost clinical eye — and then the prose does something extraordinary.
"We had never seen such dissatisfied children. It was not merely that they were weazened and shrivelled—though they were certainly that too—but they looked absolutely ferocious with discontent."
"Ferocious with discontent" — that's a phrase nobody had ever written before, and nobody has quite managed since.
And then he goes further — when the Tockahoopo Indians are mentioned, Egbert gives Esther a frown so savage she genuinely mistakes him for one.
It's a children's version of pure malice — and it is absolutely hilarious.
I'd want to note that the comedy there is doing something quite pointed about Mrs. Pardiggle's particular brand of philanthropy.
These are children who have been conscripted into charitable giving — their pocket money, their autonomy, their childhood essentially stripped away in the name of doing good.
"The face of each child, as the amount of his contribution was mentioned, darkened in a peculiarly vindictive manner."
"Vindictive" is exactly right — these boys know they've been wronged, even if they can't name it.
Dickens sees coercive charity as a form of violence — and he puts that violence on the faces of children so we can't look away.
There's also that last detail — "the little recruit into the Infant Bonds of Joy, who was stolidly and evenly miserable."
"Stolidly and evenly miserable" — the youngest one has already given up.
He doesn't have the energy left for ferocity — he's just settled into a baseline of despair.
And it's funny — genuinely, wickedly funny — but it also breaks your heart a little.
That tension — between the comedy and the cost of it — seems central to how Dickens builds his grotesques.
Oliver, there's another comic portrait I'd love to bring in — Mr. Jarndyce's extraordinary evasions of gratitude.
Jarndyce is one of Dickens's most perfectly constructed comic characters precisely because his eccentricity is rooted in genuine goodness.
He cannot bear to be thanked — and his methods of avoiding it escalate to a kind of sublime absurdism.
There's this wonderful anecdote Ada recalls — her mother went to Jarndyce's house to thank him for some great kindness.
"He happened to see her through a window coming to the door, and immediately escaped by the back gate, and was not heard of for three months."
Three months.
He didn't just leave the room — he vanished from recorded existence for a quarter of a year.
The joke is perfect because it escalates at exactly the right speed — and then it stops before it tips over.
What I love is the children's response to this story — they don't find it alarming, they find it completely charming.
And Esther says they talked of scarcely anything else all day — returning to it over and over, wondering about Jarndyce, imagining what he'd say.
"All of which we wondered about, over and over again."
It's such a simple line, and it captures exactly the excitement of being young and on the way to somewhere new and possibly wonderful.
Dickens earns his warmth — it never feels imposed.
I'd gently push back on the word "charming" — because Jarndyce's flight from gratitude is also a flight from accountability.
He does good — genuinely, I think Dickens means us to believe that — but he does it on his own terms, anonymously, without the social obligation that gratitude creates.
The benevolent patriarch who vanishes before the thanks arrive is still controlling the terms of the relationship.
I'm not saying Dickens intends that — I don't think he does — but it's latent in the portrait nonetheless.
Daniel, I think you're absolutely right — and that's what separates Dickens from a sentimentalist.
The comic portrait always contains a shadow — something that complicates the easy feeling.
It's exactly why the novel's final grotesque image of Sir Leicester works so strangely — because he's ridiculous, but the prose gives him grandeur.
Listen to this — the ancestral portraits at Chesney Wold speak to him, and Dickens gives them the most hauntingly beautiful voice —
"Each of us was a passing reality here and left this coloured shadow of himself and melted into remembrance as dreamy as the distant voices of the rooks now lulling you to rest."
It's magnificent — and it's put in the mouths of the ancestors of a man Dickens is satirising with cold fury.
That's the kind of thing that makes you put the book down and simply stare at the ceiling for a moment.
"Coloured shadow" — it's such a precise image for a portrait.
A portrait is literally a coloured shadow — and Dickens uses it to collapse the line between presence and erasure.
Sir Leicester is being compared to his ancestors and simultaneously diminished by them — he too will melt into remembrance.
The satire is buried so deep inside the beauty you almost don't feel the knife.
Beauty as a vehicle for the knife — that's a wonderful formulation.
Let's end this section with what I think might be the most concentrated piece of Gothic-comic writing in the whole novel — Mrs. Snagsby.
Mrs. Snagsby is one of the great unsung comic creations in all of English fiction — and that closing passage in Chapter Twenty-Five is where she becomes something more than comic.
She begins the chapter as a jealous wife — absurd, suspicious, comic in her paranoia.
And then Dickens does something astonishing — he transforms her into a shadow.
"And henceforth he begins, go where he will, to be attended by another shadow than his own, hardly less constant than his own, hardly less quiet than his own."

"And into whatsoever atmosphere of secrecy his own shadow may pass, let all concerned in the secrecy beware! For the watchful Mrs. Snagsby is there too—bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh, shadow of his shadow."
"Bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh" — that's the language of the marriage vow turned inside out and made Gothic.
The comedy has become fate — she's not just a suspicious wife, she is his inescapable shadow.
The Biblical language is doing real work there — "bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh" — because it invokes the marriage covenant as a binding legal and moral contract.
Mrs. Snagsby has no recourse in law — divorce was essentially unavailable, women had no independent legal standing.
Her surveillance is the only power she has — and Dickens recognises that, even while he satirises her obsession.
"The watchful Mrs. Snagsby" — she watches because watching is all she's been left.
And it begins with her as "a ghostly shade, frilled and night-capped" — that's the image we start with.
The domestic detail — the frill, the nightcap — sits right up against the Gothic register of "ghostly shade," and the collision is both funny and slightly terrifying.
That's what I mean when I say Dickens earns his effects — every word is in exactly the right place.
You don't get one without the other — the comedy needs the Gothic, and the Gothic needs the comedy.
The comedy needs the Gothic, and the Gothic needs the comedy — I think that might be the defining formula of Bleak House's genius.
Thank you all — we'll pick up in a moment with the novel's deeper architecture of justice and injustice.

segments.title: Jo's Story: Marginality and the Cost of Invisibility

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've been circling the great institutions of this novel — the Court of Chancery, the aristocracy, the philanthropic establishment.
In this segment we turn to those the system makes invisible: Jo the crossing-sweeper, the women of the slums, the dead man in the ruined room.
I'm joined as ever by Oliver Trevelyan, the actor and audiobook narrator who hears this novel as a performance before anything else.
By Dr. Daniel Rosen, our cultural historian who reads every institution in the novel as a machine for protecting the powerful.
And by Caroline Woodcourt, our close reader and book critic, who has re-read this novel more times than she'll readily admit.
Daniel, let's begin with you — because the passages we're looking at today put the cost of poverty in absolutely unsparing terms.
Yes — and Dickens doesn't sentimentalise it, which is what makes these passages so remarkable.
In the scene where Esther and Ada visit the brickmaker's cottage, a baby dies.
Dickens gives it to us in exactly five words.
"As she did so, I saw what happened and drew her back. The child died."
That's the whole sentence. That's the whole event.
No funeral, no named grief, no memorial paragraph — the prose simply moves on, as society moves on.
The brevity is the argument.
That compression is devastating on the page — and I've never been able to read it aloud without something catching in the throat.
But what strikes me equally is what comes just after — Esther watching the two women comfort each other.
Dickens gives Esther a moment of real moral perception there.
She writes: "I think the best side of such people is almost hidden from us.
What the poor are to the poor is little known, excepting to themselves and God."
That last phrase — "excepting to themselves and God" — is doing something quite unusual for Dickens.
He's saying that the inner life of the poor is simply beyond the reach of observation — including his own.
It's an act of narrative humility that stops you cold — coming from a novelist famous for knowing everything about everyone.
And then you turn to the inquest scene in chapter eleven, and it's as if the novel takes a great theatrical breath.
Mrs. Piper — goodness, Mrs. Piper.
She testifies — and I use the word loosely — in what Dickens describes as "chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation."
The whole speech is one magnificent, cascading run-on sentence.
She insists on calling the deceased "the plaintive" — which is both a malapropism for plaintiff and a rather poignant accident of meaning.
The dead man is the plaintive. He just can't say so anymore.
Oliver's right that the comedy is brilliant — but the comedy is doing political work as well.
What Mrs. Piper's testimony actually establishes is nothing about the dead man except rumour and fear.
He was strange, he was solitary, he had a ferocious air — therefore he was suspect.
This is exactly how the law treats the poor: their character is established by hearsay, their lives weighed by people who never actually knew them.
And then comes Jo — and everything shifts.
Jo is the one witness who actually knew the man — who had a real encounter with him — and the novel gives that encounter such quiet force.
The scene is this: a cold winter night, Jo shivering in a doorway, and the man — Nemo, as we come to know him — turns back.
He finds that Jo has not a friend in the world.
"Neither have I. Not one!" and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging."
Two friendless people, finding each other in a doorway.
That's the whole of their connection — and somehow it's everything.
When you read that aloud, the exclamation mark on "Not one" is not triumphant — it's desolate.
It's a man recognising himself in a starving boy, and the recognition is worse than the poverty.
Dickens also tells us that Nemo asked Jo whether he ever wished to die — which is an extraordinary thing to put in.
These are men for whom the fundamental question is no longer how to live, but whether to.
And while Jo and Nemo share that doorway, elsewhere in the novel Vholes is operating his machine of professional duty.
Vholes is a lawyer — and Dickens's portrait of him is one of the coldest satirical achievements in all his work.
He hides cruelty entirely inside the language of obligation.
To Esther he says — and I want you to hear the full throttle of this — "I HAVE carried it out; I do carry it out.
But I will not smooth things over to any connexion of Mr. C.'s on any account.
I regard it in the light of a professional duty to be so, though it can be charged to no one."
"Though it can be charged to no one" — that's the masterpiece.
The destruction of Richard Carstone is performed as a free service, out of pure integrity.
And the moment he finishes this magnificent self-justification, Richard walks in — and Vholes turns on sixpence.
"Am I here, sir? Yes, I thank you; I am here, Mr. C., and enjoying the pleasure of some agreeable conversation with Miss Summerson."
The absolute, untroubled velocity of that switch — from doom to pleasantry — is the funniest and most frightening thing.
There is no inner life to interrupt the performance.
Which brings us full circle, doesn't it — back to Esther's line about the poor.
Nemo and Jo have interior lives that exceed anyone's capacity to observe them.
Vholes has professional performance where an interior ought to be.
The novel keeps asking: who gets to be seen, and who defines what seeing even means?
That question — who gets to be seen — is one we'll keep returning to, because Dickens keeps returning to it.
After the break, we'll follow that thread into the fog itself — and into the legal labyrinth that gives this novel its peculiar, suffocating atmosphere.

segments.title: Reading the Unreadable: Lady Dedlock's Secret and Narrative Withholding

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel apart sentence by sentence — and finds more in it each time.
Today we're deep inside one of the novel's most sustained acts of narrative sleight of hand — the slow, terrible emergence of Lady Dedlock's secret.
Dickens withholds, deflects, and surrounds his central mystery with watching eyes and impenetrable surfaces.
With me to take it apart are Oliver Trevelyan, the man who has probably read more Dickens aloud than anyone since Dickens himself.
Daniel Rosen, cultural historian, who reads every secret in fiction as also a secret about power.
And Caroline Woodcourt, critic and close reader, who knows better than anyone what it feels like to encounter these passages for the first time — and the twentieth.
Let's begin where so much of the novel's tension begins: in a drawing room, with Sir Leicester reading a letter aloud.
What I love about that scene — Sir Leicester fumbling with his eye-glass, losing his place — is that Dickens builds the dread through pure comic delay.
The reader already knows something terrible is coming, and here is Sir Leicester hunting through the letter for the right paragraph.
There's a stage direction buried in the prose: 'my Lady looks a little irritated.'
'My Lady looks a little irritated.'
That understatement is doing everything — she is a woman on the edge of catastrophe, and Dickens gives her 'a little irritated.'
And then finally the letter delivers its blow, wrapped in all the formal courtesy of Tulkinghorn's prose.
'I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him.'
Three words at the end. 'I have seen him.' The sentence is a trap door.
And the trap door opens without a sound, which is exactly what makes it so frightening.
Sir Leicester reads the words aloud — he's the one delivering the blow — and he has no idea.
That's the cruelty of Dickens's arrangement. The most oblivious person in the room is also the instrument.
And then in the scene that follows, Dickens shows us what happens between Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn — which is precisely nothing, on the surface.
He writes: 'Lady Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn, without any other alteration in their customary deportment, have looked very steadily at one another.'
'Without any other alteration in their customary deportment.'
Every syllable of that phrase is armour. Theirs, and his.
What strikes me is who isn't watching in that scene.
Sir Leicester, we're told, has looked at the fire — 'with the general expression of the Dedlock on the staircase.'
'With the general expression of the Dedlock on the staircase.'
He becomes, in that moment, a portrait — an institution rather than a person.
The aristocracy isn't watching because it doesn't need to watch. It trusts its lawyer to do that.
Tulkinghorn doesn't serve Sir Leicester out of loyalty. He serves him because holding secrets is the source of his power.
Dickens makes this absolutely explicit when he describes Tulkinghorn approaching across the terrace.
'He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress.'
The man is a vault. He has absorbed the secrets of the ruling class into his very physical form.
And that description — 'every limb of his body and every crease of his dress' — it's such a physical image for something entirely internal.
When I read Tulkinghorn aloud, I always slow right down. He's the one character in the novel where the pace of the prose itself becomes oppressive.
Dickens even tells us: 'his usual methodical pace, which is never quickened, never slackened.'
'Never quickened, never slackened.'
That rhythm is the man. Reading it aloud, you feel the inexorability — there is no escape from this pace.
He is his own client in the matter of his soul, and he will never betray himself. That is genuinely chilling.
What Dickens does in the passage describing their subsequent meetings — the dinners, the days — is extraordinary to me as a reader.
He gives us the social surface, perfectly rendered.
'Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine.'
That phrase — 'exhausted deity' — is one of the great compressed portraits in all of Dickens.
She is worshipped. She is bored by the worship. She cannot escape either condition.
And then Dickens pivots to the interior — everything we cannot see.

'Whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows — all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts.'
He refuses to go inside. He builds the interior as a set of unanswered questions, and then seals the door.
That passage is formally remarkable, but I want to push on what it conceals politically.
The two parties watching each other are not equal. Tulkinghorn holds professional power over Lady Dedlock — he is the instrument through which her secret can be deployed as a weapon against her.
The syntax of 'whether each... whether each... what each' creates a false symmetry. Dickens writes as though the balance of power is genuinely uncertain.
But it isn't. She is a woman with a secret. He is a man with an institution behind him.
And this connects directly to what Jarndyce eventually tells Esther about her origins — the absolute, enforced silence around Lady Dedlock's identity.
'She was, if there were any ties of blood in such a case, the child's aunt. That more than this she would never — for any human consideration — disclose.'
The secret isn't just shame — it's the absolute condition of her survival within the aristocratic order.
Daniel's right about the power imbalance, and yet — as a performer — what stays with me is the sheer theatrical discipline of Lady Dedlock herself.
She is performing 'exhausted deity' for her life. Literally.
And Dickens gives that performance its due — 'insolent grace' is the phrase when she passes Tulkinghorn in the doorway.
'She passes close to him, with her usual fatigued manner and insolent grace.'
'Insolent grace.' Two words that contain an entire self-possession in the face of total danger.
That phrase captures something essential — Lady Dedlock's capacity to make her concealment into a form of dignity.
And what's remarkable is that Dickens sustains this — the not-knowing, the watching, the sealed hearts — across hundreds of pages.
Next we'll turn to what this secret costs — the people it destroys, beginning at the margins, where secrets always do their worst work.

segments.title: The Music of Suffering: Dickens on Death and Loss

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the show where we read Dickens slowly, carefully, and with great pleasure.
Today's segment takes us somewhere that Dickens handles with extraordinary skill: the music of suffering — the way he frames loss, foreboding, and the slow collapse of a life.
We have three brilliant companions for this conversation.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more classic novels than anyone alive, and he hears Dickens the way a conductor hears a score — every pause is deliberate, every rhythm is chosen.
Dr. Daniel Rosen reads the novel as an anatomy of class and power — and he'll show us today that even the tenderest moments are shaped by social forces.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a critic who reads with her whole self — she'll tell us what stops you mid-sentence and makes you read a line again.
We begin with a passage that is outwardly one of the most tender in the novel: Mr. Jarndyce blessing the young love between Richard and Ada.
But Esther, watching all of this, ends the scene with an image so quietly devastating it feels like a tolling bell.
Oliver, you've read this scene aloud more than once — where does it live for you?
It lives in the repetition, which is where Dickens always hides the feeling.
Jarndyce says "afar off" twice in the space of a breath, and each time the phrase does different work.
The first time it's a gentle disclaimer — I saw this possibility, but only from a distance.
The second time — and this is where you have to perform it right, or you lose the whole effect — it's almost a warning.
Let me read the whole passage so we can hear it properly.
"I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the possibility of you and your pretty cousin here — don't be shy, Ada, don't be shy, my dear! — being in a mind to go through life together."
"I saw, and do see, many reasons to make it desirable. But that was afar off, Rick, afar off!"
That second "afar off" — it's a sigh dressed as a sentence.
Jarndyce knows something the children don't — that distance is not a circumstance but a permanent condition of his feeling for Ada.
And then Esther takes that tenderness and darkens it — quietly, almost without you noticing.
The passage at the close of the scene is one of those moments I've returned to again and again.
Esther watches them pass through the sunlit room and describes them with this heartbreaking beauty.

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness."
Three "so"s in a row — it's incantatory, almost liturgical.
And then: "So they passed away into the shadow and were gone."
That fourth "so" turns the whole thing.
It sounds like a continuation of the hymn — and then it becomes an elegy.
"The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
Dickens doesn't explain. He simply closes the door and turns off the light.
What I'd add is that the light and shadow aren't just poetic atmosphere — they're socially determined.
Richard and Ada are walking toward Jarndyce and Jarndyce.
The shadow that falls over them is the shadow of the Court of Chancery — an institution that exists to consume young men exactly like Richard.
But notice what Jarndyce does in the scene Oliver read from — he is extraordinarily careful not to wield power.
He says it explicitly, almost as a disclaimer.
"I have no power over you whatever."
But of course, that statement is itself an exercise of power — the power of the guardian who defines the terms of affection.
Benevolent patriarchy is still patriarchy — and Dickens, to his immense credit, shows us the mechanism even when he clearly loves Jarndyce.
That's entirely true — and it sharpens how you play Jarndyce on the page.
The "chain of flowers" line is the comic Dickens and the dark Dickens in a single breath.
He says the chain of flowers they've taken up is "very easily broken" — and then adds — "or it might become a chain of lead."
It's a joke. But only barely.
By the time we reach the end of Richard's story, you hear that line again in your head — and the flowers are long gone.
There's a passage about Lady Dedlock that brings a very different kind of collapse — and the prose is almost brutally sudden.
Where the Richard and Ada scene moves slowly, beautifully, like the light fading — Lady Dedlock's ruin arrives all at once.
The narrator opens the passage with a single word that feels like a verdict.
"So! All is broken down."
Two syllables of contempt — "So!" — and then everything is rubble.
And the sentence that follows doesn't pause for breath.
"Her name is in these many mouths, her husband knows his wrongs, her shame will be published — may be spreading while she thinks about it."
Each clause lands like another blow.
What destroys me is that little parenthetical: "may be spreading while she thinks about it."
Time itself is now her enemy — shame moves faster than thought.
And notice what the novel stacks at the end of that sentence: she is "denounced by an invisible accuser as the murderess of her enemy."
She hasn't committed the murder — but at this moment, the accusation is almost beside the point.
The system of shame and exposure has already executed her in the public eye before any court has even convened.
This is how class operates in the novel — it doesn't need formal procedure.
Lady Dedlock was protected by class on the way up. It destroys her on the way down.
And the omniscient narrator — "So! All is broken down" — sounds less like a novelist and more like the voice of the system delivering its sentence.
The contrast in narrative voice is extraordinary, isn't it.
When Esther watches Richard and Ada walk into the sunlight, the prose is tender, almost maternal — you feel Esther's love in every syllable.
When the omniscient narrator turns to Lady Dedlock, the voice is cold, relentless — it doesn't flinch.
Two narrators, two registers of suffering — and Dickens uses both to make sure no character escapes the full weight of what the novel is about.
The genius is that neither feels false.
That dual narrator structure — Esther's intimate grief and the omniscient narrator's cold reckoning — is something we'll return to throughout the series.
For now, what strikes me most from this conversation is how Dickens uses light and shadow not as decoration but as argument — the sun clouds over, and we know without being told.
My thanks to Oliver, Daniel, and Caroline for a conversation as rich as the novel itself.
We'll be back with the next segment of Bleak House Unpacked very shortly.

segments.title: Redemption and Remainder: What Bleak House Leaves Us

utterances.text: We've spent this episode tracing the great machinery of Bleak House — its law, its fog, its losses.
Now, in our final segment, I want to ask what Dickens leaves us with — what survives the wreckage.
There are characters in this novel who are given every chance — and squander it.
And there are institutions that absorb every reforming impulse and spit it back as self-congratulation.
Oliver, I want to start with Richard Carstone — a young man who is given very direct, very good advice, and cannot take it.
Richard Carstone is one of those characters who breaks your heart precisely because you can see, at every stage, exactly what he should do.
And John Jarndyce — good, patient, long-suffering Jarndyce — sees it too.
There is a moment where he lays it all out for Richard with extraordinary directness.
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner."
And then he goes further — this is the part that stops me every time —
"If you had the abilities of all the great men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely meaning it and setting about it."
That phrase — sincerely meaning it — is the whole of Richard's tragedy in four words.
He never quite means it. Not because he is wicked, but because Chancery has given him a reason not to.
What I find almost unbearable about that speech is that Richard hears it.
He really does hear it, and he says so. And then he goes away and does the opposite.
He confesses it himself — later, to Esther, with real shame — and the passage is almost painful to read.
"I wish to heaven I were a more constant sort of fellow... not constant to Ada, for I love her dearly — but constant to myself."
Constant to myself. There it is. The self-knowledge that arrives too late to be useful.
And what strikes me is that Dickens does not let Richard off. There is no last-minute recovery. The novel is honest about what inconstancy costs.
I don't disagree with any of that — but I want to be careful about where we place the blame.
Richard's inconstancy is a character flaw — but it is a flaw that Chancery cultivates deliberately, in people like Richard, because it profits from their paralysis.
And Dickens shows us exactly how this self-perpetuating system protects itself from reform.
The passage about Vholes and the Parliamentary inquiry is one of the most savagely funny pieces of writing in the entire novel.
A committee asks whether these legal forms occasion delay. The attorney admits: yes, some delay.
Great expense? Most assuredly they cannot be gone through for nothing.
And then the killer blow — the answer that, as Dickens tells us, proved fatal to the inquiry for ten years —
"Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a MOST respectable man."
Respectability. That is the whole arsenal. That is all you need.
The MOST is capitalised in the original text — Dickens actually capitalises it — and that capital letter is doing enormous work.
You can hear the attorney straightening his waistcoat as he delivers it.
And Kenge does the same earlier — he doesn't even bother to deny that the law is hard.
He says to the client — with magnificent condescension —
"I understand your present feelings against the existing state of things, which I grant to be a little hard in your case."
A little hard. A little hard! The man is being ruined by this system and Kenge calls it a little hard.
And what Dickens understood — and what makes this novel as relevant now as in 1853 — is that this is not corruption in the ordinary sense.
No one in that passage is lying. Vholes is probably, in the terms of his profession, a thoroughly diligent man.
The system does not require villains. It requires respectable men who keep it running.
And Richard Carstone — who is also, in his way, a respectable young man — is the human cost of keeping it running.
Richard goes to Chancery looking for a future, and Chancery consumes him. That is what the novel insists upon.
And yet — and this is what I keep coming back to — Jarndyce's words to Richard do not become wrong just because Richard cannot follow them.
That speech survives Richard's failure. It survives Chancery.
Dickens is not naive about systems — Daniel is absolutely right about that.
But he still believes that effort and sincerity are the answer — even when the system is designed to defeat them.
That tension is what gives the novel its ache. It refuses easy despair and it refuses easy comfort.
The world is before you, Jarndyce tells Richard. And it most probably will receive you as you enter it.
It is the most generous sentence in the book — and the most devastating, in retrospect.
Because it is true. The world does receive Richard exactly as he enters it — which is without constancy, without purpose, with only hope and charm.
Dickens gives us the instruction manual for a good life, and then shows us, in exquisite detail, a young man who cannot open it.
There is something almost Shakespearean in that — the truth spoken clearly, heard clearly, and still not acted upon.
Bleak House does not end in triumph — but it does not end in pure despair either.
What it leaves us with is something harder to name: a deep accounting of what is lost when systems devour people, and a quiet insistence that the alternative remains possible.
My thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, Daniel Rosen, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that has, I hope, done some justice to this extraordinary novel.
For all of us on Bleak House Unpacked — thank you for listening.

c43:p23.text:
We went upstairs to the first floor, still seeing no other furniture
than the dirty footprints. Mr. Jarndyce without further ceremony
entered a room there, and we followed. It was dingy enough and not at
all clean, but furnished with an odd kind of shabby luxury, with a
large footstool, a sofa, and plenty of cushions, an easy-chair, and
plenty of pillows, a piano, books, drawing materials, music,
newspapers, and a few sketches and pictures. A broken pane of glass
in one of the dirty windows was papered and wafered over, but there
was a little plate of hothouse nectarines on the table, and there was
another of grapes, and another of sponge-cakes, and there was a
bottle of light wine. Mr. Skimpole himself reclined upon the sofa in
a dressing-gown, drinking some fragrant coffee from an old china
cup—it was then about mid-day—and looking at a collection of
wallflowers in the balcony.
c43:p23.summary: Skimpole's sitting room is filthy and deteriorated yet paradoxically filled with luxurious furnishings, musical instruments, fruits, and wine—a perfect emblem of his irresponsible aestheticism.
c43:p23.best_quote: It was dingy enough and not at all clean, but furnished with an odd kind of shabby luxury, with a large footstool, a sofa, and plenty of cushions, an easy-chair, and plenty of pillows, a piano, books, drawing materials, music, newspapers, and a few sketches and pictures.

c58:p105.text:
Very familiar to him, as he said himself some hours ago, George
Rouncewell lifts him into easier positions through the long remainder
of the blank wintry night, and equally familiar with his unexpressed
wish, extinguishes the light and undraws the curtains at the first
late break of day. The day comes like a phantom. Cold, colourless,
and vague, it sends a warning streak before it of a deathlike hue, as
if it cried out, “Look what I am bringing you who watch there! Who
will tell him!”
c58:p105.summary: George tenderly attends Sir Leicester through the long night; dawn breaks colorless and deathlike, the refrain 'Who will tell him!' echoing as the day arrives with the specter of tragedy.
c58:p105.best_quote: "The day comes like a phantom. Cold, colourless, and vague, it sends a warning streak before it of a deathlike hue, as if it cried out, 'Look what I am bringing you who watch there! Who will tell him!'"

c24:p154.text:
The sun was down, the light had gradually stolen from the roof, and
the shadow had crept upward. But to me the shadow of that pair, one
living and one dead, fell heavier on Richard’s departure than the
darkness of the darkest night. And through Richard’s farewell words I
heard it echoed: “Of all my old associations, of all my old pursuits
and hopes, of all the living and the dead world, this one poor soul
alone comes natural to me, and I am fit for. There is a tie of many
suffering years between us two, and it is the only tie I ever had on
earth that Chancery has not broken!”
c24:p154.summary: Esther reflects on Gridley's final words, which echo through her memory and Richard's departure, reinforcing the novel's commentary on Chancery's destructive power.
c24:p154.best_quote: Of all my old associations, of all my old pursuits and hopes, of all the living and the dead world, this one poor soul alone comes natural to me, and I am fit for. There is a tie of many suffering years between us two, and it is the only tie I ever had on earth that Chancery has not broken!

c9:p49.text:
“By my soul,” exclaimed Mr. Boythorn, suddenly firing another volley,
“that fellow is, and his father was, and his grandfather was, the
most stiff-necked, arrogant imbecile, pig-headed numskull, ever, by
some inexplicable mistake of Nature, born in any station of life but
a walking-stick’s! The whole of that family are the most solemnly
conceited and consummate blockheads! But it’s no matter; he should
not shut up my path if he were fifty baronets melted into one and
living in a hundred Chesney Wolds, one within another, like the ivory
balls in a Chinese carving. The fellow, by his agent, or secretary,
or somebody, writes to me ‘Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, presents
his compliments to Mr. Lawrence Boythorn, and has to call his
attention to the fact that the green pathway by the old
parsonage-house, now the property of Mr. Lawrence Boythorn, is Sir
Leicester’s right of way, being in fact a portion of the park of
Chesney Wold, and that Sir Leicester finds it convenient to close up
the same.’ I write to the fellow, ‘Mr. Lawrence Boythorn presents his
compliments to Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, and has to call HIS
attention to the fact that he totally denies the whole of Sir
Leicester Dedlock’s positions on every possible subject and has to
add, in reference to closing up the pathway, that he will be glad to
see the man who may undertake to do it.’ The fellow sends a most
abandoned villain with one eye to construct a gateway. I play upon
that execrable scoundrel with a fire-engine until the breath is
nearly driven out of his body. The fellow erects a gate in the night.
I chop it down and burn it in the morning. He sends his myrmidons to
come over the fence and pass and repass. I catch them in humane man
traps, fire split peas at their legs, play upon them with the
engine—resolve to free mankind from the insupportable burden of the
existence of those lurking ruffians. He brings actions for trespass;
I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and
battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha,
ha!”
c9:p49.summary: Boythorn launches an elaborate account of his escalating disputes with Sir Leicester over a right of way, detailing the volleys of letters, his theatrical retaliation with a fire engine, his destruction of gates, and the counter-actions in law, all recounted with relish and concluding with triumphant laughter.
c9:p49.best_quote: He brings actions for trespass; I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha, ha!

c62:p58.text:
“That is what I mean,” said my guardian. “You may observe, Mr.
Bucket, that I abstain from examining this paper myself. The plain
truth is, I have forsworn and abjured the whole business these many
years, and my soul is sick of it. But Miss Summerson and I will
immediately place the paper in the hands of my solicitor in the
cause, and its existence shall be made known without delay to all
other parties interested.”
c62:p58.summary: John Jarndyce explains that he will not examine the will himself because he has long abandoned the Chancery suit as morally repugnant, but he will immediately submit it to his solicitors.
c62:p58.best_quote: The plain truth is, I have forsworn and abjured the whole business these many years, and my soul is sick of it.

c17:p19.text:
“My dear Miss Summerson,” she replied, “on Mr. Carstone’s character
and conduct. He is of such a very easy disposition that probably he
would never think it worth while to mention how he really feels, but
he feels languid about the profession. He has not that positive
interest in it which makes it his vocation. If he has any decided
impression in reference to it, I should say it was that it is a
tiresome pursuit. Now, this is not promising. Young men like Mr.
Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can
do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a
very little money and through years of considerable endurance and
disappointment. But I am quite convinced that this would never be the
case with Mr. Carstone.”
c17:p19.summary: Mrs. Badger elaborates that Richard lacks the positive interest in medicine that sustains practitioners through hardship, unlike Mr. Woodcourt whose commitment comes from genuine passion.
c17:p19.best_quote: Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment.

c55:p71.text:
“Hush! Hush!” The housekeeper looks round and answers in a frightened
whisper, “My Lady, I have not breathed a word of it, I don’t believe
what’s written in it, I know it can’t be true, I am sure and certain
that it is not true. But my son is in danger, and you must have a
heart to pity me. If you know of anything that is not known to
others, if you have any suspicion, if you have any clue at all, and
any reason for keeping it in your own breast, oh, my dear Lady, think
of me, and conquer that reason, and let it be known! This is the most
I consider possible. I know you are not a hard lady, but you go your
own way always without help, and you are not familiar with your
friends; and all who admire you—and all do—as a beautiful and
elegant lady, know you to be one far away from themselves who can’t
be approached close. My Lady, you may have some proud or angry
reasons for disdaining to utter something that you know; if so, pray,
oh, pray, think of a faithful servant whose whole life has been
passed in this family which she dearly loves, and relent, and help to
clear my son! My Lady, my good Lady,” the old housekeeper pleads with
genuine simplicity, “I am so humble in my place and you are by nature
so high and distant that you may not think what I feel for my child,
but I feel so much that I have come here to make so bold as to beg
and pray you not to be scornful of us if you can do us any right or
justice at this fearful time!”
c55:p71.summary: Mrs. Rouncewell delivers a long, passionate plea to Lady Dedlock, urging her to conquer her pride and help clear her innocent son if she knows any truth or clue.
c55:p71.best_quote: My Lady, you may have some proud or angry reasons for disdaining to utter something that you know; if so, pray, oh, pray, think of a faithful servant whose whole life has been passed in this family which she dearly loves

c51:p64.text:
He was leaning on his arm saying these words in a meditative voice
and looking at the ground when my darling rose, put off her bonnet,
kneeled down beside him with her golden hair falling like sunlight on
his head, clasped her two arms round his neck, and turned her face to
me. Oh, what a loving and devoted face I saw!
c51:p64.summary: Ada rises and kneels beside Richard with her golden hair cascading over him, embracing him devotedly and turning her face toward Esther.
c51:p64.best_quote: my darling rose, put off her bonnet, kneeled down beside him with her golden hair falling like sunlight on his head, clasped her two arms round his neck, and turned her face to me

c1:p1.text:
Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and
meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers
of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city.
Fog on the Essex marshes, fog on the Kentish heights. Fog creeping
into the cabooses of collier-brigs; fog lying out on the yards and
hovering in the rigging of great ships; fog drooping on the gunwales
of barges and small boats. Fog in the eyes and throats of ancient
Greenwich pensioners, wheezing by the firesides of their wards; fog
in the stem and bowl of the afternoon pipe of the wrathful skipper,
down in his close cabin; fog cruelly pinching the toes and fingers of
his shivering little ’prentice boy on deck. Chance people on the
bridges peeping over the parapets into a nether sky of fog, with fog
all round them, as if they were up in a balloon and hanging in the
misty clouds.
c1:p1.summary: Fog blankets London from the Thames to the marshes, penetrating every space and afflicting everyone from Greenwich pensioners to cabin boys, creating an all-encompassing sense of obscurity and misery.
c1:p1.best_quote: Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city.

c8:p55.text:
We had never seen such dissatisfied children. It was not merely that
they were weazened and shrivelled—though they were certainly that
too—but they looked absolutely ferocious with discontent. At the
mention of the Tockahoopo Indians, I could really have supposed
Egbert to be one of the most baleful members of that tribe, he gave
me such a savage frown. The face of each child, as the amount of his
contribution was mentioned, darkened in a peculiarly vindictive
manner, but his was by far the worst. I must except, however, the
little recruit into the Infant Bonds of Joy, who was stolidly and
evenly miserable.

c6:p9.text:
The notes revived in Richard and Ada a general impression that they
both had, without quite knowing how they came by it, that their
cousin Jarndyce could never bear acknowledgments for any kindness he
performed and that sooner than receive any he would resort to the
most singular expedients and evasions or would even run away. Ada
dimly remembered to have heard her mother tell, when she was a very
little child, that he had once done her an act of uncommon generosity
and that on her going to his house to thank him, he happened to see
her through a window coming to the door, and immediately escaped by
the back gate, and was not heard of for three months. This discourse
led to a great deal more on the same theme, and indeed it lasted us
all day, and we talked of scarcely anything else. If we did by any
chance diverge into another subject, we soon returned to this, and
wondered what the house would be like, and when we should get there,
and whether we should see Mr. Jarndyce as soon as we arrived or after
a delay, and what he would say to us, and what we should say to him.
All of which we wondered about, over and over again.

my Lady, with broad strips of sunlight shining in, down the long
perspective, through the long line of windows, and alternating with

words, for I happened afterwards to note them in my diary, which is
producible at any time—I mentioned to you that Mr. C. had laid down
the principle of watching his own interests, and that when a client
of mine laid down a principle which was not of an immoral (that is to
say, unlawful) nature, it devolved upon me to carry it out. I HAVE
carried it out; I do carry it out. But I will not smooth things over
to any connexion of Mr. C.’s on any account. As open as I was to Mr.
Jarndyce, I am to you. I regard it in the light of a professional
duty to be so, though it can be charged to no one. I openly say,
unpalatable as it may be, that I consider Mr. C.’s affairs in a very
bad way, that I consider Mr. C. himself in a very bad way, and that I
regard this as an exceedingly ill-advised marriage. Am I here, sir?
Yes, I thank you; I am here, Mr. C., and enjoying the pleasure of
some agreeable conversation with Miss Summerson, for which I have to
thank you very much, sir!”

my memory. I beg you’ll excuse me. He
 says—”  Sir Leicester is so

c12:p114.text:
During the utterance of every word of this short dialogue, Lady
Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn, without any other alteration in their
customary deportment, have looked very steadily at one another—as
was natural, perhaps, in the discussion of so unusual a subject. Sir
Leicester has looked at the fire, with the general expression of the
Dedlock on the staircase. The story being told, he renews his stately
protest, saying that as it is quite clear that no association in my

c12:p67.text:
At length, one afternoon a little before sunset, when the bright
groups of figures which have for the last hour or two enlivened the
Ghost’s Walk are all dispersed and only Sir Leicester and my Lady
remain upon the terrace, Mr. Tulkinghorn appears. He comes towards
them at his usual methodical pace, which is never quickened, never
slackened. He wears his usual expressionless mask—if it be a
mask—and carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every
crease of his dress. Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great
or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his
personal secret. He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients;
he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.

The door stood open, and we both followed them with our eyes as they
passed down the adjoining room, on which the sun was shining, and out
at its farther end. Richard with his head bent, and her hand drawn
through his arm, was talking to her very earnestly; and she looked up

beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through

had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun
was clouded over.

“Well!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “That’s rational. Now, hear me, my dears!
I might tell you that you don’t know your own minds yet, that a

well this chain of flowers you have taken up is very easily broken,
or it might become a chain of lead. But I will not do that. Such
wisdom will come soon enough, I dare say, if it is to come at all. I
will assume that a few years hence you will be in your hearts to one
another what you are to-day. All I say before speaking to you
according to that assumption is, if you DO change—if you DO come to
find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and
woman than you were as boy and girl (your manhood will excuse me,
Rick!)—don’t be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be
nothing monstrous or uncommon in it. I am only your friend and
distant kinsman. I have no power over you whatever. But I wish and
hope to retain your confidence if I do nothing to forfeit it.”

c13:p118.text:
“Come!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “Now for our assumption. Now we lift our
eyes up and look hopefully at the distance! Rick, the world is before
you; and it is most probable that as you enter it, so it will receive
you. Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never
separate the two, like the heathen waggoner. Constancy in love is a
good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy
in every kind of effort. If you had the abilities of all the great
men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely
meaning it and setting about it. If you entertain the supposition
that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could
be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts,
leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here.”

c39:p4.text:
But not perceiving this quite plainly—only seeing it by halves in a
confused way—the laity sometimes suffer in peace and pocket, with a
bad grace, and DO grumble very much. Then this respectability of Mr.
Vholes is brought into powerful play against them. “Repeal this
statute, my good sir?” says Mr. Kenge to a smarting client. “Repeal
it, my dear sir? Never, with my consent. Alter this law, sir, and
what will be the effect of your rash proceeding on a class of
practitioners very worthily represented, allow me to say to you, by
the opposite attorney in the case, Mr. Vholes? Sir, that class of
practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth. Now you
cannot afford—I will say, the social system cannot afford—to lose
an order of men like Mr. Vholes. Diligent, persevering, steady, acute
in business. My dear sir, I understand your present feelings against
the existing state of things, which I grant to be a little hard in
your case; but I can never raise my voice for the demolition of a
class of men like Mr. Vholes.” The respectability of Mr. Vholes has
even been cited with crushing effect before Parliamentary committees,
as in the following blue minutes of a distinguished attorney’s
evidence. “Question (number five hundred and seventeen thousand eight
hundred and sixty-nine): If I understand you, these forms of practice
indisputably occasion delay? Answer: Yes, some delay. Question: And
great expense? Answer: Most assuredly they cannot be gone through for
nothing. Question: And unspeakable vexation? Answer: I am not
prepared to say that. They have never given ME any vexation; quite
the contrary. Question: But you think that their abolition would
damage a class of practitioners? Answer: I have no doubt of it.
Question: Can you instance any type of that class? Answer: Yes. I
would unhesitatingly mention Mr. Vholes. He would be ruined.
Question: Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a respectable
man? Answer:”—which proved fatal to the inquiry for ten years—“Mr.
Vholes is considered, in the profession, a MOST respectable man.”
c39:p4.summary: Mr. Kenge's rhetorical defense of legal practitioners like Vholes is presented, along with a mock parliamentary inquiry that demonstrates how institutional self-interest defeats reform through the invocation of Vholes's respectable reputation.
